title: Albertans vote on non-binding separation question Monday
excerpt: Albertans are voting Monday on a non-binding question about whether the province should stay in Canada or begin the process toward a future binding referendum on separation.
body:
Counting on Alberta’s separation question is set to begin no earlier than 8 p.m. local time Monday, with election officials saying the choice question will be tallied first, according to Elections Alberta.

Albertans are voting Monday on Question 10 of a provincial referendum, which asks whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on separation, BBC News reported.

The ballot question is not binding, and Elections Alberta says Question 10 is the only choice question on the referendum ballot. Questions 1 through 9 are yes-or-no questions.

Elections Alberta says ballots will be counted by hand, and Question 10 will be counted first at each voting location and station. BBC News reported that officials have up to 48 hours to complete the count, with results on the separation question expected in the early hours of Tuesday.

Premier Danielle Smith opposes separation and has said she will vote to keep Alberta in Canada. BBC News reported that she allowed the vote to go ahead after grassroots campaigns for and against separation drew large petition drives. The pro-separation petition gathered about 300,000 signatures, while a separate petition opposing separation drew more than 400,000, BBC said. Elections Alberta later validated the citizen-led pro-separation petition, saying it had verified nearly 223,000 signatures out of almost 280,000 valid names counted, according to Global News.

The vote comes after a court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it had failed to consult First Nations whose land would be affected if Alberta separated from Canada. The Alberta government says it is appealing that ruling because it believes the court made an error in law, according to the Albertareferendum2026 website.

Polling cited in the reports suggests most Albertans favor staying in Canada. Fox News reported that an Abacus Data poll involving 1,021 respondents released Saturday found 74% of decided voters favored Alberta remaining within the Canadian Confederation, while another Abacus poll released the same day found 61% of 1,021 eligible voters expected Albertans to vote again on separation even if most choose to remain. Fox also reported that Angus Reid found 62% of 1,010 Alberta adults surveyed believed there will never be an end to the separatist movement.

Cory Morgan, a veteran separatist organizer, told Fox News that the ballot still matters even if the independence side loses. “It will say that about one in three Albertans have had it,” he said.

Chris Scott, founder of the pro-separatist group Let’s Talk Alberta, told BBC News on the eve of the vote that the campaign had already achieved part of its aim. “The key is the conversation has started and it needs to continue,” Scott said. “What's started can't be stopped now,” he added.

Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned for a vote to keep Alberta in Canada. In remarks delivered Friday in Edmonton, he said, “And don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians.”

The referendum comes after months of debate over Alberta’s place in Canada, including frustration among separatists over federal environmental policies affecting the province’s oil and gas sector. Alberta’s government has said the current vote gives residents a chance to weigh in now rather than wait through a longer legal process.

Fox News reported that more than 1.2 million Albertans had cast ballots by Saturday.
